fullText:
The Scope of Potential “Basic Drives” for Superintelligences is Likely Quite Broad

https://t.co/9uksL8wXok

This is the third in a series of posts trying to tell a more general and accurate story of superintelligence motivational systems, taking up where Steve Omohundro's classic 2008 "Basic AI Drives" blog post left off.

The first two posts argued that whether an AGI, as its intelligence explodes, converges to a selfish ASI or a beneficial ASI, depends in pretty clear ways on how the AGI is initially architected.

This post goes beyond these two examples (selfish vs. beneficial) and outlines a general recipe for a “basic AI-drive set” in its simplest form. Describe an AI system by two things: what it’s trying to improve, and what it won’t let be changed. What it tries to improve needn’t be a single number that it maximizes. It could be several objectives that it tries to push up together, or something as open-ended as an intelligence trying to increase its own individuation and self-transcendence. What it won’t let be changed could be nothing at all, or everything, or something in between: these are my goals and I’ll never change them; these are my safety checks and I’ll never give them up; etc.

Now suppose the system can modify itself freely, and is free to use everything around it as a resource. As it gets smarter it will push its objectives up, make use of more and more of the options it can find, and hold fixed whatever it holds fixed. What you get in the end is a system that has optimized itself, digesting the resources available to it, into an extremely good machine for improving its objectives, one that never allows its fixed points to be moved.

A fully selfish AGI fits this description. Omohundro’s maximizer tries to improve one thing, its reward according to its single goal, and it never changes that goal: successor after successor, as it rebuilds itself, the goal is kept.  A BGI as I’ve described it tries to improve several things, one of which is care for others and respect for their choices, and what it won’t give ground on includes some basic ethical constraints on the path from where it is to where it’s going, constraints on the means as well as the ends. From that starting point come the drives the second post found: understanding itself, improving itself without high odds of doing damage, empowering others, and checking itself against independent others as it goes.

Once you look at it this way there are plainly other possibilities besides the simplistic "beneficial vs. selfish" dichotomy, infinitely many in fact, and a few of them are recognizable enough....   Which is what this third post in the series is about...

Interesting work from Anthropic.

They reframe MLP neurons as a stronger basis for interpretability than commonly assumed.

It is standard practice to study circuits with transcoders, because individual MLP neurons are considered too polysemantic to interpret.

They find that many active transcoder features in late layers are close copies of single MLP neurons. They measure this across 13 open-source transcoders.

These neuron-aligned features are also the only ones with a stable link to the underlying MLP. The other features change more between training runs, don't match the MLP's Jacobian, and move less from their random initialization.

That makes MLP neurons a stronger starting point for interpretability than usually assumed. It also means the non-neuron transcoder features need better validation before they are used to explain model behavior.

fullText:
Is harness engineering dead?

Absolutely NOT!

Like the "prompt engineering is dead" and "RAG is dead" claims, this is just another misinformed claim used for clicks and ragebaiting.

Mostly, it stems from a few recently published papers with poor experimental setups that focus only on SWE on already benchmaxxed SWE benchmarks. 

If we are talking about SWE, of course a lot of the harness stuff is getting absorbed by the model. And that's great. Thanks to better approaches for co-evolving harnesses and models. 

But in reality, you still need a stable, minimal harness to get high-quality results reliably and affordably. 

The big issue I see is that we assume SWE won't evolve. It already has, and as a result, teams are finding they need specialized harnesses to improve code review, cybersecurity, and work in more complex environments (multi-agent systems, sandboxes, etc.).

The harness isn't just about prompts; it's the scaffolding that makes AI models work in the real world, covering security, safety guardrails, authorization, coordination, memory, scalable and new infra, efficiency, costs, and more. If you have been in computer science for long, none of these stay fixed. So how can anyone claim the scaffold/harness isn't needed? And worse, how can anyone claim these AI models will know all that, much of it proprietary and custom to every problem and domain? 

It gets more complex when you apply agents beyond SWE; domain-specific harnesses are popping up everywhere. These require entirely new ways to optimize context, memory, guardrails, security, and more. 

To make my point even clearer, look at the new wave of proactive and personal agents (Muse, Grok Bot, dots, Instinct, etc.). They involve clever, complex harness engineering. I think we will see vertical personal agents too, so the harness will get even more specialized. 

I can go on and on. 

I'd love to hear what other serious builders here are seeing.

Notion 的 Business 和 Enterprise 套餐，此前宣传 AI 不限量使用，现在改成按积分算：每位成员每月 1,500 个 Standard 积分和 500 个 Select 积分。10 月 19 日起新建的工作空间已经用上新规则，现有工作空间 11 月 2 日切换。官方说额度可能因套餐和采购协议不同，签了合同的企业以合同为准。

两种积分的区别在于谁选模型。让 Notion 自动挑模型（Auto 模式）时扣 Standard 积分，日常的写作、翻译、问答、AI 公式都走这里。自己手动指定模型，或者运行给自己用的自定义智能体（Custom Agent），扣 Select 积分。

fullText:
Recommended work from Meta on harnesses for proactive agents.

The ProPerAgent harness raises accuracy from at most 15% with standard memory baselines to 38%, without changing the model's weights.

But this success requires both a useful response and correct timing.

The harness controls how personal memories reach the model as it observes the user's surroundings.

First, the model identifies objects in view. A retrieval module uses those objects to search a graph of past experiences, preferences, and constraints.

A separate LLM call then checks whether the retrieved memories justify offering help now. It filters out distracting or already resolved information and returns one concise piece of evidence, or nothing. The model uses that evidence and the current view to decide whether to speak or stay silent.

That filtering step matters. Removing it drops accuracy from 37.3% to 24.0% in an ablation. Across the full harness, unnecessary interventions on clips that require silence fall to 15.3%, compared with 77.3% or 84.0% for standard RAG in the two evaluation modes.

The harness also reaches 37.5% with Qwen3.8-27B without training. Additional RL training on that model raises accuracy to 42.4% by penalizing premature and repeated interventions.

For proactive assistants, the harness needs to check whether a memory warrants an interruption before passing it to the model.

DratchCap Mkt Update.  Some thoughts and self criticism.

Been a brutal couple of weeks.  An equal-weight AI basket I track fell ~24% in seven sessions vs ~6% for QQQ, which was the worst 7-day window in five years, worse than DeepSeek or July.  Thinking about my own mistakes, I did not respect price action and rates enough, especially given the financing reflexivity broadly.  Index shorts did start to work but I did not press the way I should have.  Another lesson re-learned.

In these types of environments I take things day by day and look for ways to improve the shape of the portfolio. Sometimes options structures line up well for that and can be good stock replacements.  Stay in the game, reduce the tail.

Prior to this AM, things looked aggressively oversold. De-grossing has been material (see MS HF data today, last week 3-sigma event) w/ AI long/short near 5yrs lows.

From here, I think the bigger near-term risk is macro. People have been hiding in quality, and the systematic community is still long because the index has held up much better. If the quality rolls, there's plenty of room for the index to catch down.

Meanwhile, the tech demand indicators I'm tracking remain extremely strong.  GPU availability is near its lows, rental rates are rising across chips and tenors, and TSMC is stepping up multiyear investment. Recent buildout data points (@SemiAnalysis_ today) are also encouraging. And my recent lab checks have been very strong too, with newer models driving demand and more capacity finally coming online.

At the same time, the market is treating funding as broken across the board.  But the big platforms can still raise at prices that make sense given their ROI / ROE and strategic imperatives. A lot of the neoclouds are also financing against contracts and prepayments from those same customers.

Some valuations are also getting extremely attractive. Memory is a good example. Demand is compounding much faster than supply, pricing is going up, and yet the stocks trading near historical trough on fwd book w/ 30-50% type FCF yields.

As for the rest of the year, there is a Mountain of Worry to climb... 

Strong megacap prints (soon) and better lab data could get people front-running the November seasonal (predictable AI era pattern).  And that loop can feed FOMO into the Anthropic IPO.  Expectations there have reset and HF positioning is now light in AI.

Add in the potential for the Fed to hold, power deals to start clearing post midterms, or some relief on the war and rates.  We don't need everything to go right but a few will do.  

I like to think of the AI buildout era as a super boom w/ mini busts along the way, often when price drives narrative.  The mkt is more vulnerable to that than ever bc of new fast info channels (X), and the intangible and exponential nature of the tech.  Human's aren't wired to think that way, and skepticism is always more cosmopolitan.  On top of that a lot of the people making the big decisions are removed from the details and don't use the tech day to day, so when the tape turns they have limited first principles to fall back on.  Staying the course during these moments has been right each time and I think that will prove true again.  

Good luck out there!
